chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
title: Hearing like a musician and defining a jazz singer
summary: She says since the 1960s she tried to move away from early style and thinks like a musician.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Yes, since the '60s. Because I did sort of try to get away from early style and that early approach. First of all you run out of material and number two, it's just a repetition of what you did before. And I think I'm doing now what I wanted to do in the first place. I'm music oriented. What I mean by that is I consider myself more of a musician than a singer so far as the equipment is concerned. I think I think

like a musician. I think I hear like a musician. And I like instrumental music. I think what I'm trying to do maybe is to either sound like an instrument or improvise like a musician would. And I think . . .
That would be your definition of a jazz singer?

Yeah. I have a tendancy, if music is playing I improvise alot with the music. If I'm listening to a recording or I'm working with a band, so much so that sometimes if I'm sitting on the sidelines and listening to somebody take a solo I'm improvising and they tell me to shut up because it's their solo. So I like to think in terms of musician more than a singer.
